output:
# 1. Reply to Jane

**Subject:** Re: Planning my parental leave (good news inside)

Hi Jane,

Congratulations! Thank you for reaching out early. It gives us plenty of time to plan.

**Good news first: you do qualify for paid parental leave.** The handbook page you found (v2023, section 7.2) is out of date, and I'm sorry it's still posted. On July 1, 2025, Policy Bulletin PB-2025-04 replaced it. Under the bulletin, you need only **6 months of continuous service on the first day of leave**. You reached that on **September 3, 2025**.

Under the current policy:

- You get **up to 16 weeks at 100% of base pay**, used within 12 months of the birth.
- You can take it in one block, or in **up to two blocks of at least 2 weeks each**.
- In New York, it runs **at the same time as NY Paid Family Leave (NY PFL)**. NY PFL pays a partial benefit, and the company pays the difference so you receive 100% of base pay. You've been eligible for NY PFL since **September 1, 2025** (26 consecutive weeks after your start date).

**Example plan: one block starting on your due date**

| Period | Dates | Pay |
|---|---|---|
| Weeks 1–12 (NY PFL + company top-up) | Mon Feb 16 – Sun May 10, 2026 | 100% of base |
| Weeks 13–16 (company paid leave) | Mon May 11 – Sun June 7, 2026 | 100% of base |
| Back at work | **Mon June 8, 2026** | |

Babies keep their own schedules, so these dates will move with the actual birth date.

**One gap:** the policy material I have covers leave *after* the birth. It doesn't cover time off *before* the birth or for medical recovery. If you think you may need to stop working before your due date, tell me and I'll get an answer from the Benefits team.

---

**1. Can I carry 10 days of PTO into 2026?**

Unfortunately, no. The PTO policy lets you carry over **up to 5 days**. Anything above 5 is forfeited on December 31.

You earn 1.25 days for each *completed calendar month*, credited at month-end. You started on March 3, so it isn't clear whether March counts as a completed month. Here are both versions:

| | If March counts | If March doesn't count |
|---|---|---|
| Months accrued in 2025 (through Dec 31) | 10 (Mar–Dec) | 9 (Apr–Dec) |
| Accrued: months × 1.25 | 12.50 days | 11.25 days |
| Less used so far | −4.00 | −4.00 |
| Balance on Dec 31 (if you take no more PTO) | 8.50 days | 7.25 days |
| Carried into 2026 (max 5) | 5.00 | 5.00 |
| **Forfeited if unused** | **3.50 days** | **2.25 days** |

I'll confirm your exact balance with Payroll. In the meantime, plan to **use about 2.25–3.5 days before December 31** so you don't lose them. A few days of rest before a new baby isn't a bad idea anyway.

In 2026, January's 1.25 days are credited on January 31. That means you could have **about 6.25 days available by mid-February**. The policy doesn't say whether PTO keeps accruing during leave, so I'll confirm that too.

Your parental leave is already fully paid, so you don't need PTO to fill a pay gap. You could add PTO *after* the 16 weeks to extend your time off. Before you do, see the job protection question in #4.

**2. Can I raise my Dependent Care FSA to the maximum now?**

Not yet, I'm afraid. You can change your election mid-year only **within 30 days after a qualifying life event**. The birth is that event; the pregnancy isn't.

- If the baby arrives February 16, your deadline would be **March 18, 2026**.
- The **2026 limit is $7,500 per household**. If a spouse or partner has a dependent care FSA elsewhere, your combined elections count toward that one limit.

Two things I'll check with Benefits for you:

- **Open enrollment for 2026.** The guide I have doesn't give the open enrollment dates. If enrollment is open now, you may be able to set your 2026 election without waiting for the birth.
- **Adding the baby to your medical plan.** You're on employee-only coverage. The guide doesn't spell out the steps or deadline for adding a newborn, and you won't want to miss it.

**3. Do I have to tell my manager yet?**

No, January works. The policy asks for **30 days' notice when leave is foreseeable**. For a February 16 start, that means **by Friday, January 16, 2026**.

My suggestion:

- **Tell your manager in the first week of January** (say, by January 9). That gives you both time to plan coverage, and it gives you a cushion if the baby comes early.
- **Send me your planned start date by January 16.**

The policy doesn't say whether notice should go to your manager, HR, or both, so I'll confirm that. Until you're ready, I'll treat what you've told me as between us.

**4. Is my job protected while I'm out?**

Partly confirmed, partly being checked.

- **Weeks 1–12 are job-protected through NY PFL.** That covers Feb 16 – May 10 in the example above.
- **FMLA won't apply at the start of your leave.** FMLA requires 12 months of service, and you'll reach that on **March 3, 2026**, two weeks after your due date. So your original plan of "PTO plus unpaid FMLA" isn't the right picture. The paid leave above replaces it.
- **Two points the policy material doesn't answer:**
  - whether weeks 13–16 of company paid leave (May 11 – June 7) are job-protected
  - whether FMLA protection begins once you reach 12 months mid-leave

  I'm asking Legal to confirm both **in writing**. Please hold off on adding PTO beyond week 16 until we have their answer.

---

**What happens next**

- **By Friday, November 14:** I'll send you answers from Payroll (PTO balance and accrual during leave), Benefits (open enrollment, newborn medical enrollment, pre-birth leave, and how to file the NY PFL claim) and Legal (job protection for weeks 13–16).
- **By December 31:** use your extra PTO days.
- **First week of January:** tell your manager.
- **By January 16:** send me your planned leave start date.
- **Within 30 days after the birth:** update your Dependent Care FSA (and medical coverage, once Benefits confirms that deadline).

Congratulations again. Reply anytime with questions, or if you'd like to talk it through.

Warmly,
[Name]
HR Generalist, Northwind Freight Systems

---

# 2. Internal note to HR policy owner

**Re: Parental leave material — fixes needed**

- **Outdated handbook:** Handbook v2023 section 7.2 is still on the intranet, although PB-2025-04 superseded it on July 1, 2025. An employee concluded she didn't qualify. Please remove it or mark it superseded.
- **PB-2025-04 gaps:**
  - It doesn't say whether weeks 13–16 (beyond NY PFL's 12) are job-protected.
  - It doesn't say who receives the 30-day notice.
  - It doesn't explain how to file the NY PFL claim.
  - It doesn't cover pre-birth or medical-recovery leave.
- **PTO policy section 6.1:** It's unclear whether a partial hire month counts as a "completed calendar month." It also doesn't say whether accrual continues during leave.
- **Benefits guide:** It omits open enrollment dates and the deadline for adding a newborn to medical coverage.
- **Legal summary:** It doesn't address an employee who reaches 12 months of service during a leave.
